LESSON - I
INDIAN ECONOMY ON THE EVE OF
THE BRITISH RULE
The most outstanding feature of the Indian economy was the existence of self-sufficient
and self-governing village communities. The disintegration of the Mughal empire in the 18th
century inevitably brought about economic disruption. The East India Company rule in India
opened a new chapter in the economic history of India. Colonial interests of the East India
Company regained supremacy over the economic needs of the Indian masses. The reader will
no doubt read the condition of Indian economy before the coming of British.

1.2 Introduction
The British rule in India unleashed far-reaching changes in Indian economic structure.
New demand of land revenue made changes in rural economy and social relationships. The
British policies developed a new era of distorted modernization, and ruined the traditional
agriculture and industry and resulted in the growing poverty of the masses. Here we are analyse
the Indian economy on the eve of the British rule.
1.3 Pre-British Economic Structure
During the pre-British period, i.e. during the mid-eighteenth century, the condition of
Indian economy was not at all satisfactory. Just after the death of Aurangzeb in 1707, the
central power at Delhi was so weak that the situation had led to disintegration and gradual
downfall of deep rooted Mughal Empire. During 1750, the Indian economy was passing through

recurrence of crisis and disorders because by this time the central power at Delhi was either
weakened or disappeared.
Indian economy, consisted of backward, isolated and self sustaining villages on the one
hand and on the other hand, a number of towns which were the seats of administration,
pilgrimage, commerce and handicrafts. During this period, the mode of transport and
communication of India were totally backward, underdeveloped and insufficient. Under such a
situation, the size of market was also very small.
Indian Economy mainly consisted of two parts – rural and urban. The economic
organization in the rural areas was rather simple. The basis of this economy was the isolated
and self- sufficient villages, where life was regulated according to well established customs
and traditions. The village population consisted of three categories of people – the agriculturists,

village officers and village artisans and menials. Almost 70 per cent of the adult population of
the village was engaged in agriculture and depended on its land for livelihood. These people
produced what was immediately needed by them and paid no attention to scientific agriculture
or increase in production. Despite this state of affairs the people were said to the contented. It
was the wealth of India which attracted a large number of invaders and foreign powers. Even
the British came to India with a view to make profits by carrying on trade with India.

3
The chief village officers were headmen or Patel, responsible for the maintenance of law
and order in the village as well as collection of revenue. The third section of the village community
consisted of hereditary artisans like carpenters, blacksmith, potter, barber, cobbler, washermen,
goldsmith, oilman, shop-keeper etc. These artisans rendered service in the various fields to
the inhabitants of the village. They were given all the necessities of life by the village. Generally
each house-holder of the village gave a share of his produce to these persons for the services
rendered by them. The number of towns was very small and the inhabitants of the towns
depended for their good supplies on the neighboring villages. They possessed an efficient
system of credit. The most common methods used for credit were hundies or bills of exchange.
1.3.1 Self-Sufficient Village Communities

The most outstanding feature of the Indian village economy was the existence of selfsufficient and self-governing village communities. Indian villages functioned as little worlds of
their own, having very little to do with the outside world. Village economy was self-subsisting,
providing the foodstuffs it needed except perhaps a few necessities like salt and iron. Another
marked feature was the union of agriculture and handicraft industry. The family of the peasant
undertook spinning and weaving as a secondary activity and produced the cloth needed for the
family. The other economic needs were also provided by village craftsmen like the carpenter,
the goldsmith, the potter, the black-smith, the oil-presser, etc., who in effect were servants of
the village and received a customary share in the village crops for their services. The basic

land relationships in the village were governed by custom and usage. The concept of private
property in land, as understood in the modern sense, did not develop. The land in the village
belonged to the cultivating community, each family having its share of arable land.

4
The village communities were self-governing. The village panchayat administered the
village affair, settled disputes and administered justice. The village Headman was its leader in
dealing with the government. The local chief or the distant subahdar did not interfere in village
affairs except claiming a share in the village crops varying from one-sixth to one-half. Political
convulsions did not disturb the placid life of village communities. Bur there was a dark side to
the stability and isolation of the village communities. The ideal of self-sufficiency acted as a
barrier to the creation of a wider market for Indian handicrafts. The closed and caste-bound
socio-economic structure permitted little horizontal, vertical or spatial mobility of labour. It
cramped human mind, stifled spirit of enterprise and became an instrument of socio-economic

stagnation. Further, the indifference to political affairs outside the village militated against the
emergence of national consciousness.
All the above mentioned occupations were hereditary. These various groups of people
were getting their remuneration in terms of crops during the harvesting period against the
services rendered by them. These Indian villages were functioning independently as most of
food articles and raw materials produced within the villages were either consumed or purchased
by the village communities itself. Agricultural and handicraft industry were interdependent and
thus the village republics were able to function independently. Indian villages were almost selfsufficient in respect of daily necessities excepting commodities like salt, spices, finecloth, luxury
and semi-luxury goods.

5
In this connection, Sir Charles Metacalfe wrote, “The village communities are little republics
having nearly everything they want within themselves, and almost independent of foreign
relations. They seem to last where nothing lasts. This union of the village communities each
one forming a separate little state by itself…………is in a high degree conducive to their
happiness, and to the enjoyment of a great portion of freedom and independence”. Thus during
the pre-British period, Indian villages were mostly consisting of three distinct classes: (a) the
agriculturists, (b) the village artisans and menials and (c) the village officials. There were again
two types of agriculturists— (a) the land owning and (b) the tenants.
1.3.2 Condition of Agriculture during the Pre- British Period
During the mid-eighteenth century, the condition of Indian agriculture was not at all

satisfactory. During those days, agriculture was the main source of livelihood in India. The
economic condition of Indian agriculturists was really very much painful. Poor farmers had to
pay a high rate of taxes as imposed by the then administrators of the country which led to high
degree of exploitation on these farmers. During those days Indian rulers had constructed and
maintained some irrigation projects but these works were very much insufficient as compared
to its requirement. Moreover, farmers were following traditional methods in their agricultural
operations. Important crops which were grown by Indian farmers included mainly rice, wheat,
bajra, jowar and minor cereals along with the commercial crops like jute, raw cotton, groundnut,
tobacco etc. Again, the crop rotation practices of standard pattern were followed without any

variation. Some strips of land were left fallow every year just for the interest of regaining fertility.
In those days, the agricultural implements were mostly primitive and simple which included
wooden plough, iron sickle, leather bag for drawing water etc. During those days, agriculturists
were applying only natural organic manures.
Thus it is better to conclude with Dr. Buchanan and Prof. Gadgil that the conditions of
Indian agriculturists in total were very much depressed. Moreover, the land policy followed by
the rulers of those days was mostly going against the farmers and these policies were specially
framed to serve the interests of rulers and zamindars of India.
1.3.3 Prices and Wages during the Pre- British period
During the pre-British period, the prices of foodgrains used to fluctuate widely between

different places. Markets for most of the commodities were very much restricted to local areas
in the absence of adequate means of transport and communications. Under such a situation,

6
agricultural produces and the other commodities produced by artisans in the cottage industries
were not getting remunerative prices. During those days, the prevailing wage rates were very
low. Wages of village artisans were paid not in terms of cash but in kind. The wages were paid
mostly once in a year and that is just after the harvesting season. The rates of wages were
mostly determined by customs and conventions.
1.3.4 Structure and conditions of Towns during Pre- British period
During the pre-British period, the major portion of the total population of India was living
in the rural areas. Nearly 10 per cent of the total population was living in the urban areas and
those towns were merely out grown villages. According to Prof. D.R. Gadgil, towns of those
days owed their existence principally due to the following three reasons: (a) A good number of

towns of India were places of pilgrimage or sacred religious centres (for example, Gaya, Benaras,
Allahabad, Puri, Nasik etc.); (b) A good number of towns were the seats of courts of Nawabs or
kings or the capital of a province (for example, Bijapur, Golconda, Delhi, Lahore, Lucknow,
Poona etc.); and (c) A good number of towns were trading or commercial centres due to its
trade importance (for example, Surat, Mirzapur, Hubli, Bangalore etc.). These towns were
existing on different trade routes. Those towns which were actually the trade centres proved
more stable.
Lifestyle in the towns was completely different from that of the villages. In these towns, a
large category of occupations and different varieties of trades were existing. Thus the sizes of
population of these towns were gradually increasing. Moreover, the size of market of these
towns was also wide.

1.3.5 Indian Industries during Pre- British Period
Although agriculture had dominated the Indian economy during the pre-British period yet
some Indian industries, producing certain special products, enjoyed worldwide reputation. During
those days, many of the handicrafts produced in the urban areas of India were quite famous.
Among all those various famous urban handicrafts, textile handicrafts earned a special status
and were also spread over the whole country. During those days, the muslin of Dacca, silk
sarees of Benaras, shawls and carpets of Kashmir and Amritsar, the calicos of Bengal, dhoti
and dopattas of Ahmedabad, silk and bordered cloth of Nagpur and Murshidabad etc. were
very famous and received much recognition in international markets.

7
While recognizing the skill of Indian artisans, T.N. Mukherjee wrote, “A piece of the
muslin 20 yards long and one yard wide could be to pass through a finger ring and
required six months to manufacture.” Moreover, India was well known for her other artistic
handicraft industries which include jewellery made of gold and silver, brass, copper and bell
metal wares, marble work, carving works in ivory, wood, stone etc. Artistic glassware were also
produced in India during those days and had earned international reputation. India had also
developed high level of metallurgy and the cast-iron pillar standing near Delhi is a real testament
of that.
All these industries and handicrafts had its patronage of local administrators for their
development. In the urban area each handicraft was properly organised into a guild so as to

safeguard their common interest. These guilds were enacting their own laws which were again
respected by the then rulers of the country. According to M.G. Ranade, the Indian industries
“not only supplied all local wants but also enabled India to export its finished products to foreign
countries.” During those days, Indian export items were consisting mostly of manufactured
items like cotton and silk fabrics, calicos, silk and woollen cloth and artistic wares made of
glass and metal. Besides, the other export items were included, pepper, opium, indigo etc.
Throughout the 17th and 18th century, European countries were purchasing the above
mentioned manufactures of India.
1.3.6 Foreign Trade during Pre- British Period
India had a very favourable balance of trade and attracted traders from various countries

of Asia and Europe. The trade was carried on both through the land routes as well as sea. The
most popular land routes for carrying on trade with the foreign countries were the route running
through North-West through Lahore and Kabul to Central Asia and the route running from
Multan and Kandahar to Persia. The sea routes which were most popular were those through
Persian Gulf and Red Sea ports in West Asia, and the Indian Archipelago and Spice Islands in
the east. The chief items exported by India included the calicoes, muslins, silks, fancy goods,
indigo, salt-petre, spices and pepper. The Indian textiles also were in great demand, especially
in countries of Asia and Europe. The chief Indian imports were gold, silver, precious stones,
horse, metals, tobacco etc.
1.3.7 Features of the Pre- British Economic Life in India

When we analyse the various features of the economic life in India on the eve of the
British rule, we note the following characteristics:

8
 Firstly, the villages which were the primary units of rural economy were self-sufficient.
This self-sufficiency was to a large extent due to the primitive and defective means of
communication.
 Secondly, agriculture enjoyed preponderance over other occupations, which inevitably
resulted in the domination of the rural over the urban population.
 Thirdly, prevelance of cottage and handicraft industries which were under the control of
independent artisans and a comparative absence of large-scale industries.
 Fourthly, in most of the areas of the country (with the exception of towns) the system of
barter prevailed. However, in the towns the money economy had made its appearance.
 Fifthly, lack of proper credit system and narrowness of the market.
 Sixthly, virtual non-interference by the state in the economic life of the community.

 Seventhly, regulation of the economy according to well established customs and statutes.

2.2 Introduction
The English East India Company had very humble beginnings in India. The Charter of
1600 granted the East India Company the exclusive privilege of trading east of the Cape of
Good Hope for a period of 15 years. The Company was a strictly closed corporation or a
monopoly. By 1623 it had established factories (trading posts) at Surat, Broach, Ahmedabad,
Agra, and Masulipatam. From the very beginning, it tried to combine trade and diplomacy with
war and control of the territory where their factories were situated. The constant flow of wealth
from India to England for which India did not get an adequate economic, commercial or material

return has been described by Indian national leaders and economists as ‘drain’ of wealth from
India. The drain of wealth was interpreted as an indirect tribute extracted by imperial Britain
from India year after year.
2.3 The British Rule and Indian Economy
The East India Company was set up under the Charter of the Queen with the sole object
of “carrying on trade in goods and products of an overseas country”. According to Rajni Palme
Dutt, it was not done with a view to find a market for the British manufactures but “to endure to
secure a supply of the products of India and the East Indies (especially spices, cotton goods
and silk goods), which found ready market in England and Europe, and could thus yield a rich
profit. As the company did not have anything to offer in exchange to India for these goods, this

resulted in the flow of the precious metals to India. As the government of Britain was not willing
to part with silver, gold and other precious metals, it impressed on the Company to devise ways
to secure the Indian goods with little or no payment. This resulted in the Company employing
pressure methods to secure the Indian goods. It resorted to the policy of territorial annexations
with a view to acquire monopoly of trade. A number of trading depots were set up in the coastal
areas, which were subsequently extended to other parts of the country as well. As a result by
the close of the seventeenth century the East India Company established its authority in almost
all the leading coastal trading centres.

12
On the assumption of administration of Bengal by the Company the field of limitless
direct plunder was opened. This excess of revenue was described as ‘investment of the
Company’ and was utilized for the purchase of Indian goods meant for export to England. With
this the long cherished dream of the Company to draw the wealth out of India without having to
give wealth in return was realised. The other features of the British policy towards India during
this period was complete neglect of irrigation and public works and destruction of Indian
manufactures coupled with policy of reckless increase in land revenue. The enormous amount
of money sent by Company to England paved the way for Industrial revolution in that country.
This gave rise to new problems of finding suitable outlets and markets for the newly manufactured

goods. Accordingly it was emphasized that the policy of mercantile capitalism should be replaced
by the policy of free trade capitalism. It was felt necessary to transform India from an exporter
of manufactured goods to an importer of manufactured goods. This was presented by the
Company, which was making huge profits due to its monopoly of trade in goods and products
of India.
In view of the ever-increasing criticism of Company’s administration the British Parliament
enacted a number of acts like the Regulating Act of 1773, the Pitt’s India Act of 1784, the
Charter Act of 1793 and the Charter Act of 1813 to establish greater control over the affairs of
the country. The Company was also forced to give up its open policy of plunder and exploitation
pursued so far and to follow a policy of reproduction of colonial economy.

13
It is evident from the above discussion that during the first phase of British rule in India,
the Company resorted to economic plunder and territorial annexations with a view to establish
monopoly of trade. It hardly paid any attention to effect improvements in administration, judicial
machinery, education system, means of communication, agriculture, industry etc. The Company
was primarily concerned with the collection of land revenue and did introduce some changes in
this field. It certainly paid no attention to the welfare of the people nor did it undertake any
projects of public welfare.
2.3.1 Free Trade Capital
A new phase in British policy towards India set in 1813 which is popularly known as the
phase of Free Trade-Capital. This phase lasted till 1857. During this phase the British not only

tried to provide an efficient system of administration but also tried to win the consent of the
governed. A number of reforms were introduced which provided for free entry to the
merchandalists, missioneries and traders of Britain in India and also introduced important
Zamindari and Ryotwari reforms. As a result of these reforms not only India’s supply of raw
materials to Britain increased but even the Indian markets for the British goods also considerably
expanded. For a fuller exploitation of the raw material resources of India, the British introduced
better means of transport and communication. English language was introduced to recruite
sufficient number of civil servants from India. Important judicial and legal reforms were also
introduced.
After the abolition of East India Company’s monopoly of trade with India in 1813, the

Indian cotton and silk goods could be sold in British markets at almost fifty per cent of the price
of the English manufactured goods. Therefore the English protagonists of free-trade resorted
to discriminatory taxation against Indian textile goods. Thereafter the Indian goods imported to
Britain were liable to 10 per cent duty against 3.5 per cent duty imposed on the import of British
cotton and silk goods imported into India. Thus it was a one-way free trade, viz. the Indian
goods were subjects to tariffs at the time of their entry into Britain, while the British goods were
permitted free entry. Through the introduction of navigation laws restrictions were imposed on
direct trade between India and foreign countries. As a result of all these measures the Indian
manufacturing Industries were destroyed. In 1850 India which had been exporting cotton goods

to various countries of the world was importing almost one-fourth of the British cotton exports.
The policy of wholesale destruction of Indian industries left a deep impact on the economy
of the country. Millions of artisans and craftsmen were rendered workless and populous
manufacturing towns like Dacca, Murshidabad, Surat etc. were rendered dissolute. The families

14
which had been formerly in state of affluence were driven to villages to find out a living. In the
villages they took to agriculture. Thus India was forcibly transformed from being a country of
combined agriculture and manufactures, into an agricultural colony of British manufacturing
capitalism. It is from this period of British rule, and from the direct effects of British rule, that
originates the deadly over-pressure on agriculture in India.
2.3.2 The Mercantilist Phase
Mercantilist ideas whish were very popular during 16th -18th centuries were an integrated
part of the old colonial system. Mercantilism was the economic counterpart of the spirit of
aggressive nationalism. The basic idea was that of regulation of all economic activity in the
interest of strengthening the nation. As far as overseas trade was concerned, it was sought to

be regulated through chartered trading companies and the twin aim was (a) to have a favourable
balance of trade (exports should be more than imports) (b) to promote flow of bullion into the
home country.
The Merchant companies aimed at a large profit-margin. This could be possible through
three methods:- (a)Monopoly control over trade and elimination of all possible rivals; (b)Purchase
of goods at cheap rates and sale of commodities at very high rates; and (c)The above objectives
could be achieved if they could establish political control over the countries they traded with.
The English East India Company’s struggle with other Merchant companies in India, viz.
the Dutch Company and the French Company, was aimed at elimination of all European rivals
from the Indian Trade. The various wars that the East India Company fought against Indian

princes – the conquest of Bengal, Anglo-Mysore wars, Anglo-Maratha wars and wars against
other Indian powers were all directed towards control of political power over various parts of
India. The political power that the Company acquired was used to control the economy of India
– to control the very sources of Indian wealth and the internal and external trade of India.
Indian merchants were prohibited not only from buying commodities directly from the producers
(which were monopolized by the English) but the agents of the Company forced their goods on
the Indian merchants at a price higher than the prevailing market price.
2.3.3 The Period of Colonial Plunder, 1757-72
The character of the East India Company underwent a change after 1757.It was no
longer merely a trading company. Henceforth, it played the role of a commercial-cum-military-

15
cum-political body in Bengal. It assumed the role of king-maker, changing Nawabs of Bengal
at will. No wonder, the Governor and members of his council engineered three quick revolutions
in Bengal (revolutions of 1757, 1760 and 1764) because each new Nawab offered fabulous
presents to the Company’s civil and military officers.
The Directors and shareholders of the Company wanted higher dividends. Even the
British government wanted a share in the new mine of gold (i.e., India) which the company had
found. Besides, while ‘farming out’ the revenue of Bengal to zamindars, the Company’s officials
received presents from the zamindars. By the sale of unauthorized dastaks (pass-chits) the
Company’s agents received bribes. The oppression of the artisans was another form of plunder;
the Company’s agents compelled the weavers to sell cloth to them at low and dictated prices.

The Company’s servants even monopolised the raw material needed by artisans and charged
a high price for them.
2.3.4 Deindustrialization
During the first half of the 19th century or even upto 1880 India’s economy witnessed a
strange phenomenon. While Western countries were experiencing industrialization, India
suffered a period of industrial decline. This process has been described as ‘de-industrialization’.
The rise of capitalism and machine-made industries which heralded the Industrial Revolution
in England and European countries gave a big jolt to handicraft industry – the price for
industrialization – in all parts of the world but the unfortunate situation in India was that unlike
the European development the decline of indigenous handicrafts in India was without the
compensating development of modern machine industry.
2.3.5 Decline of Indian Handicrafts

India’s traditional handicraft industry decayed beyond recovery. The period of decline of
Indian handicrafts was contemporaneous with the firm foundation of the Industrial Revolution
in England and England’s tight control over the strings of Indian economy.
The peculiar situation in India – very different from the developments in European countries
and North America – may be summarized thus: (a) Nineteenth century India witnessed a steep
decline of handicrafts, a process which continued well into the 20th century, and (b) Unlike
European countries India was not compensated by a sufficient rise of modern Industry. As a
result there was a net decline in the number and proportion of the Indian population engaged
in industry.

2.4 The Drain of Wealth from India
The constant flow of wealth from India to England for which India did not get an adequate
economic, commercial or material return has been described by Indian national leaders and
economists as ‘drain’ of wealth from India. The drain of wealth was interpreted as an indirect
tribute extracted by imperial Britain from India year after year
2.4.1 Concept of Economic Drain
In the mercantilist concept of trade an economic drain takes place if gold and silver flow
out of the country as a consequence of an adverse balance of trade. In the 50 years before the

battle of Plassey (1757), the East India Company had imported bullion worth £ 20 million into
India to balance the exports over imports from India. British mercantilists were highly critical of
the trade policies of the Company. Even the British government adopted a series of measures
to restrict or prohibit the imports of Indian textiles into England. Apart from other measures, in
1720 the British government forbade the wear or use of Indian silks and calicoes in England on
pain of a penalty of £ 5 for each offence on the weaver and of £ 20 on the seller.
After Plassey the East India Company extended its territorial aggression in India and
began to administer territories and acquired control over the surplus revenues of India, the
shape of drain underwent a change. Henceforth the Company had a recurring surplus which

accrued from (a) profits from oppressive land revenue policy, (b) profits from its trade resulting
from monopolistic control over Indian markets, and (c) exactions made by the Company’s
officials. All this ‘surplus’ was used by Company as an “investment”, India did not get anything
in return. This system was brought to an end by the Charter Act of 1813 when the territorial and
commercial revenues of the Company were separated.
From 1813 onwards economic drain took the form of ‘unrequited exports. Barring a few
exceptional years, favourable balance of trade had been the normal feature of our foreign

17
trade till the outbreak of World War II. The focal point of the Drain Theory was that a portion of
the national product of India was not available for consumption for her people or for capital
formation, but was being drained away to England for political reasons- and India did not get
an adequate economic return for it.
2.4.2 Economic consequences of the Drain
Dadabhai Naoroji described the drain of wealth as the “evil of all evils” and the main
cause of Indian poverty. He maintained that Britain was “bleeding India white”. In a letter to
Sunderland in 1905, Naoroji wrote, “The lot of India is a very sad one. Her condition is that of
master and a slave; but it is worse; it is that of a plundered nation in the hands of constant
plunderers with the plunder carried away clean out of the land. In the case of plundering raids

occasionally made on India before the English came the invaders went away…The British
invasion is continuous and the plunder goes right on”. Comparing the plundering raids of medieval
rulers with the British methods of colonial plunder, another critic has pointed out that the old
time plunder had to restrict himself to rich men’s houses and godowns where the wealth was
accumulated; it was not worthwhile ransacking very little hut and little village. In contrast, the
colonial plunder could reach the most lowly, the most humble and the most remote. Thus,
British methods of exploitation though less painful were more thorough and resembled the
blood-sucking leeches.
The drain of wealth checked and retarded capital accumulation in India, thereby retarding
the industrialization of India. Indian products and treasure drained to England without adequate

18
return was of great help in creating conditions in that country conducive for the growth of
British factory industry in the early stages of the industrial revolution. What is worse is that the
part of the British capital entered India as Finance Capital and further drained India of her
wealth. Naoroji complained, “British India’s own wealth is carried out of it and then that wealth
is brought back to it in the shape of loans, and for these loans she must find so much for
interest, the whole thing moving in a most vicious and provoking circle”. The drain had an
immense effect on income and employment potential within India.
Naoroji also referred to the ‘moral drain’ which, according to him, consisted in the exclusion
of Indians, from positions of trust and responsibility of their own land. He wrote, “All the talent

and nobility of the intellect and soul, which nature gives to every country is to India a lost
treasure. There is, thus a triple dwarfing or stunting of the Indian race is going on under the
present system of administration”.
In the historical perspective, the Drain of wealth theory high-lighted the foreign and
exploitative characters of British rule in a language within the comprehension of the average
Indian. During our Freedom Struggle the Drain theory became a convenient slogan for any
damnation of British colonial rule in India.

(i) Trade policies with the objective of developing a colonial pattern of trade in which India
became an exporter of primary products like raw materials and food stuffs and an importer of

malpractices; and (iv) Forcing India for paying the costs of British administration and also to
finance the wars and expeditions conducted by the British Government.

an agricultural country with a scope for commercialisation of agriculture so as to serve
the interests of Great Britain.

2. Although India was an industrially advanced country during the 16th and 17th century but

3. The British developed some forms of economic infrastructure such as electricity work,

3.2 Introduction
The British domination over Indian land started in the 18th century and the British rule
extended over large areas with the fall of Mughal empire, defeat of the Marathas and subjugation
of local powers. The British inherited the institutional form of agrarian system from the Mughals.
The British superimposed a system over the existing pattern in tune with British customs and
laws relating to land. Different land revenue systems were introduced in various part of British
India, as the British annexed different parts of India in various periods. Let us have introspection

into three broad land revenue systems introduced by the British. These land revenue systems
are Zamindari system, Rywotari System and Mahalwari System.
3.3 Pre-British Agrarian Structure
In the pre-capitalist stage of Indian economy, the idea of absolute ownership of land did
not exist. All classes connected with land possessed certain rights. The cultivator possessed
the right to cultivate and enjoyed security of tenure on the condition of payment of more or less
fixed share of produce of the year to the overlord. The Patil or the village head-man acted as
the mamlatdar or the collector (and magistrate and head farmer also) and passed on the state
demand of land revenue (which varied from 1/6th to 1/3rrd of the rental value) to the ruler or the
Nawab. The internal village arrangement connected with cultivation, allotment of the same

categories of land to certain categories of cultivators, provision of irrigation facilities, allocation
and collection of land revenue from individual cultivators, etc., were settled by the Patil in
consultation with the village Panchayats according to local customs and practices.
3.4 British Land Revenue System and Administration
The British conquerors of India sought to derive the maximum economic advantage from
their rule in India. British Industrial and mercantile interests (by advocating Free Trade principles)
prevented the East India Company from raising any substantial revenue from high custom

23
tariffs. The Company’s government in India had, therefore, to rely on land revenue as the
principal source of income for the State. As such land revenue matters received the maximum
care of the new colonial rulers.
Early British administrators of the East India Company considered India as a vast estate
and acted on the principle that the Company was entitled to the entire economic rent, leaving
to the cultivators merely the expenses of cultivation and wages of their labour. Village
communities were disregarded. In almost all parts of the Company’s territories the early
administrators resorted to the ‘farming’ of land revenues. Excessive land revenue demands
proved counter-productive. Agriculture began to languish, large areas went out of cultivation
and famines stared the people in the face. This necessitated some serious thinking, both in

India and England, about land revenue matters. Some policy decisions emerged from serious
deliberations.
3.4.1 New Land Tenures
The words land tenure (tenure is derived from the Latin word teneo i.e., to hold) are used
to refer to the conditions on which land is held by the zamindar/cultivator from the state or the
cultivator from the landlord. The English adopted three types of land tenures in India viz., the
Zamindari tenure, the Mahalwari tenure, and the Ryotwari tenure. Permanent zamindari
settlements were made in Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Benares Division of the U.P., Northern Carnatic
and roughly covered 19% of the total area of British India. The Mahalwari tenure was introduced
in major portions of the U.P., the Central Provinces, the Panjab (with variations) and covered

24
nearly 30% of the area. The Ryotwari settlements were made in major portions of Bombay and
Madras Presidencies, in Assam and some other parts of British India covering roughly 51% of
the area. The British rulers adopted various forms of land tenure in India.
3.4.2 Zamindari System
This system had been in existence in India since the times of the Mughals. Under this
system the feudal lord known as Zamindar, obtained the land from the emperor on the promise
to pay a stipulated sum of revenue. The Zamindars acquired the right to rule over the people
residing within their jurisdiction. When the Mughal Empire declined, and the authority of the
Mughal Emperor ceased to be effective, these Zamindars became dependent on the Provincial
Governors or Subahdar for their rights. Under this system the land was held by the Zamindars

who were responsible for payment of land revenue to the state. The actual cultivation was
however done by the tenants.
The English acquired the first Zamindari from Nawab Azimush Sham in 1697 over the
estates of Calcutta, Gobindapur and Satanati. The Company appointed Ralph Sheldon as the
first Zamindar for these estates. This change was significant in so far as for the first time a
foreign Zamindar was appointed who was chiefly concerned with the making of money. This
marked the beginning of a new phase in the land relations in India viz. the overlordship of land
shifted from the aristocratic class to the moneyed class.

25
A further change in the Zamindari system was introduced in 1759 when the East India
Company threw open the Zamindaries to public auction and estates were given to the highest
bidder. In this auction most of the Banyas favourably competed for the Zamindaries, and made
huge profits. They literally robbed the farmers and often forced them to abscond to escape
exorbitant revenue claims. Most of the new zamindars came from the urban rich classes and
were not interested in agriculture. They began to treat land as a commodity.
After the acquisition of Dewani of Bengal in 1765, the Company tried to make quick
gains and started charging exorbitant revenues. They gave out the zamindaries to the highest
bidders in public auction. They also started the practice of collecting the revenue directly from
the farmers in violation of the well established customs under which this was considered to be

the prerogative of the zamindars. In short, the British collected revenue from the farmers when
they were able to pay and from the zamindars when the farmers could not pay. As a result of
this policy most of the old benevolent Zamindars were deprived of their estates and the same
passed into the hands of the new class of zamindars. These new Zamindars were neither
interested in agriculture nor industry and their chief motive was to make as much money as
possible. They fully co-operated with the East India Company in the plunder. According to
Romesh Dutt as a consequence of this policy “the country grounds were put under economic
tyranny; the revenue failed once more; the system was introduced not to ameliorate the economic
condition of the rural people rather to squeeze out the last drop which left the trail of misery,
insurrections and famines in Bengal, Benaras and Oudh.”

This policy of tyranny and plunder resulted in an acute famine in Bengal in 1770 which
took a heavy toll of human life. It is estimated that roughly 35 per cent of the population died,
and almost one third of the cultivable land lay waste. The waste area increased to almost 50
per cent in 1776. This marked the beginning of long-drawn process of suffering for the people
of Bengal. There was strong resentment among the people against the foreign oppression.
They even rose against the Indian collaborators with the foreign rulers. This resulted in rebellion
of the Sanyasis in the latter half of the eighteenth century. This revolt by the innocent peasants
marked the beginning of a new awakening or consciousness and was an attempt to free the
country from alien subjugation.
3.4.3 Permanent Settlement of Lord Cornwallis

It was in this atmosphere that Lord Cornwallis introduced the system of Permanent
Settlement in 1793. By a proclamation issued on 22 March 1793 he declared the decennial

26
Settlement of Bengal and Bihar as permanent. The Zamindars were given proprietary rights in
the soil subject to the condition that they regularly paid the revenue to the Government. As a
result the owners were dispossessed of their hereditary lands and the ownership of the soil
passed into the hands of the Zamindars who had so far been merely agents of the Government
for the collection of revenues. In other words they became the owners of big estates which
never belonged to them.
The permanent settlement was introduced with three objectives in mind. First of all,
Cornwallis wanted to stabilize the hitherto uncertain and fluctuating income. The permanent
settlement could ensure to the Company a certain minimum of revenue, irrespective of the
conditions prevailing in the country. It could also save the Company expenses involved in
periodic revision of the revenue.

Secondly, they wanted to create a loyal class of proprietors who would be interested in
the continuance of the British dominion and support it at the time of trial. The Preamble to the
Regulation clearly stated that the landlord who was secure “in the quiet enjoyment of profitable
estate could have no motive for wishing for a change. On the contrary, if the rent of his lands
were raised – he will readily listen to any offers which are likely to bring about a change.” In
simple language this landed aristocracy which had withstood against the surging revolutionary
thought in Europe was expected to be the bulwark against the nationalist thought in India.

27
The third and the most important objective of introducing the permanent settlement was
that the Company wanted to divert the money capital accumulated in the hands of the new
class of urban rich into agricultural channels. Motivated by selfish considerations the British
wanted to make India an agricultural appendage of England and a market for her manufactures.
Therefore they were keen to destroy the existing manufactures in India and to block the possible
development of modern industry in India. If the money capital accumulated in the hands of the
new class of urban rich was not transferred to agricultural channels, the industrial revolution in
India could not be held in check for long.
3.4.4 Assessment of the Zamindari System
There is no unanimity among scholars and experts regarding the Permanent Settlement.

Marshman hailed the permanent settlement as a “bold, brave and wise measure.” Romesh
Dutt was also all praise for the settlement. He observed that “if the prosperity and happiness of
a nation be the criterion of wisdom and success; Lord Cornwallis’ permanent settlement of
1793 is the wisest and most successful measure which the British nation has ever adopted in
India”. On the other hand Beveridge condemned the settlement as a great ‘blunder’ and a
gross ‘injustice’. “Though the ‘permanent settlement’ helped to make the province wealthier
and most flourishing in India, it was a temporary phase and was accomplished at the cost of
millions of peasants and Indian economy. No measure can be considered good if it does not
hold good for general people. Rather it was the perpetuation of exacting spirit of the Company

Government. The land revenue collection had become the severest and exceeded in volume
from all times of the past. It had increased from 14,245,461 in 1728 to 26,800,989 in 1790-91.
The British administrators with an eye over their investment, oblivious of the interests of ryots,
preferred this peak collection and make it final and permanent.”
3.4.5 The demerits of the Zamindari system
Firstly, it placed the ryot completely at the mercy of the Zamindars who did not hesitate
to extort the last ounce of blood. So far the cultivators had enjoyed definite rights in the soil as
well as certain communal privileges with regard to homestead plots, to the pasture and forest
lands, tanks, etc. They were deprived of all these rights. Further the Zamindars got the right to
arbitrarily increase the rents, which had so far been restricted by customary rates known as
Pargana Rates.

28
Secondly, the pressure created on the agricultural land in the wake of declining cottage
industries, provided fresh opportunities of exploitation to the Zamindars. The landlords were
assured of their revenue even if the crop failed. As a result the landlords continued to grow
while the tenants were obliged to pay both the rent and the tax. This indeed made their lot
miserable.
Thirdly, the system failed to protect the rights and privileges of the tenants and they
were completely left at the mercy of heartless landlords. The landlords, unmindful of the
customary rights of the tenants, evicted them at the slightest pretext. No steps were taken till
1859 to protect the tenants against the whims of the landlords. Even thereafter, this protection
proved a farce as the tenants because of their poverty could not take recourse to legal course.

Further, it was not always possible to prove before the courts that the landlord had acted in a
highhanded manner. Thus the rights of the ryots virtually disappeared and they were rendered
helpless. As a result of this oppression some of them left the lands and became dacoits.
Fourthly, the Zamindari system led to the subdivision of rights in land. The Zamindars
did not deal with the tenants directly and leased out their interests to middle-men, who also did
likewise and thus created a long chain of intermediaries – the Talukdar, the Patindar, the
Parpatindar etc., between the State and the tiller of the soil. Simon Commission noted the
existence of about 50 intermediaries between the State and the actual tiller.
Fifthly, as a result of the permanent settlement the income of the state was permanently

fixed and it was not promised any share in the ever expanding income of the Zamindar. This
operated in favour of the Zamindars. They revised their rents several times and thus made
huge fortunes. According to S.M. Hussain a member of the Flood Commission, the net income
of the Zamindars increased from Rs.20 lakhs in 1793 to 832 lakhs in 1940.
Sixthly, the system was defective in another way too. It deprived the government of the
opportunity of knowing the rural conditions intimately. The Government lost all contact with the
ryot and hardly possessed any knowledge of the local conditions and customs. Handicapped
by these factors the government could not adopt any measures for the improvement of agriculture
or the agriculturists.
Seventhly, the Zamindari system failed to meet the growing needs of food and raw

materials of a developing economy. By keeping the ryots below the subsistence level, it greatly
restricted the internal market. It also dried up the fountain which could have been a source of
economic surplus, so vital for investment and development.

29
Eighthly, the system was to a large extent responsible for the famines which visited the
country during the closing year of the eighteenth century and the first half of the nineteenth
century. While the tiller of the land did not have any resources to invest in the improvement of
the soil, the Zamindars were not interested in investing the necessary funds for the purpose,
because they were hardly interested in the improvement of the land.
Ninthly, the system produced far reaching social consequences. The ever rising debts
of tenants and their frequent evictions created tensions in the social relations. The village
community was divided into two sections – the rich and powerful landlords and the poor and
starving peasants. The relations between these two sections were far from cordial. The ryots
had nothing but a feeling of hatred and revenge against the landlords who had dispossessed

them of their land. On the other hand the landlords also feared the ryots, whose property had
been bestowed on them. This mutual distrust gave rise to tension and upset the peace and
stability of the village life.
According to Ram Gopal the Zamindari system was “one of the great wrongs – one of the
most enormous blunders – by which 20 million small holders were dispossessed of their rights
and handed over, bound hand and foot, to the tender mercies of a set of exacting rack-renters.”
3.4.6 Ryotwari System
The second type of land settlement effected by the English was Ryotawari system. While
the Permanent (Zamindari System) was adopted in Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Bengal and North

30
Madras, the Ryotwari system was introduced in Sothern Madras, Bombay, Behar, East Punjab
and parts of Assam and Coorg. Under this system the ryot was directly under the state and the
land revenue was assessed on each separate holding and the land revenue assessed thereon.
The ryot was recognized as the proprietor and his right to sublet, mortgage or transfer by gift or
sale was also accepted. He could not be ejected from his land so long he paid the stipulated
assessment. It may be noted that the Ryotwari settlement was of a temporary nature and its
duration varied from 20 to 40 years in different parts. The credit for introducing this system is
given to Captain Read and Thomas Munro, who for the first time introduced in the districts of
Bara Mahal in 1792. Gradually the system was extended to other parts of the country. However,

certain scholars contend that the Ryotwari village was the original type of India.
A number of merits were claimed for the Ryotwari system by its authors. Firstly, it was,
said that it would establish a direct contact between the cultivator and the state. Secondly, by
conceding proprietary rights in the ryot it provided an incentive to them to make an investment
in land and its improvement. Thirdly, the system would establish self-confidence and selfreliance among the peasantry and greatly contributed to the development of cordial relations
among the various sections of the village community. Finally, under the system it would be
possible for the government to help the ryots during difficult times by reducing its land revenue
demand.
However, these merits claimed for the system proved a farce in actual practice. The

state proved no better than the Zamindars and tried to extract maximum out of the peasants by
constantly increasing the assessment. Further, the rents in the Ryotwari areas were already
high. The insatiable greed of the British ruler to extract maximum revenue from the ryot physically
and economically ruined them. As R.C. Dutt has observed, “Nature set a limit which the cultivators
had not obtained from the moderation of their rulers. Population decreased in Bombay and still
more in Central Provinces. Miles of cultivated land became waste. Jungle grew on homesteads,
wheat land and rice lands.” The law did not accord any protection to the ryot against the
arbitrary powers of the settlement officers.
The frequent upward revision of revenue by the state officials left very little scope for
improvement of lands by private owners. They did not pay attention to improvement due to the

fear that this would automatically lead to upward revision of revenue. This naturally adversely
effected the agricultural development. Highlighting this point R.C. Dutt says: “A system of
periodical settlement, which enables the state to derive profits from improvements made by
private owners, is the surest bar to all improvements.”

31
The high revenue demands also forced the ryots to borrow money from the moneylenders to discharge their liabilities. This indebtedness ultimately forced the ryots to sell their
lands. This explains the large scale transfer of land from the agriculturists to the non-agriculturists.
This in turn led to the conversion of peasants to the position of labourers or share-croppers.
They worked for the money-lenders and paid the major portion of their produce to the moneylender either in the shape of rent, interest on debt, etc. In short the system instead of producing
a class of self-reliant peasant proprietors rendered them helpless victims of the money-lenders.
The Ryotwari system by making the settlement with the individual cultivators greatly
undermined the importance of the village community as an economic unit and destroyed the

collective basis of its life. However, it cannot be denied that the Ryotwari system was different
from the Zamindari system in two different respects. First, under the Zamindari system, the
ryot did not enjoy the right to sell or transfer the land. On the other hand under Ryotwari system
the bigger peasant proprietors were free from these limitations. In this sense they possessed
an advantage over the occupancy ryots under the Zamindari system. Secondly, the occupancy
rights in the Zamindari areas were favourably placed than the Ryotwari peasants because
better irrigation facilities existed in the Ryotwari areas than Zamindari area. As a result the
Ryotwari peasants were able to retain some surplus after discharging their liabilities.
3.4.7 Mahalwari System
The Mahalwari System was introduced in 1833 by Lord William Bentinck. The genesis of

this system has best been explained by John Stuart Mill. He says that under the Mahalwari
System “the peasants-proprietors compound with the state for a fixed period. The proprietors
do not engage individually with the government but by villages. The village, through the headman,
undertakes to pay so much for so many years, they assigning to each man his quota. Primarily

32
each man cultivates and pays for himself but ultimately, he is responsible for his co-villagers
and them for him; they are ultimately bound together by joint responsibility. If one of them is
compelled to sell his rights to meet demands upon him, others have the right for pre-emption.”
In other words under this system the ownership of the entire village area was claimed by the
body of co-sharers. The village was the smallest unit and there was communal ownership of
village property. This system was first adopted in Agra and Oudh and was later on extended to
the Punjab. The procedure, period of settlement and assessment of land revenue differed from
place to place for example in Agra the settlement was made collectively with the village bodies
while in Oudh it was made with the individual Taluqdars', in Punjab the revenue was collected

from the joint-holders of the village estates. In Madhya Pradesh the Malguzars were virtually
considered the proprietary land-lords of the villages. In a way this system very much resembled
the Ryotwari. Thus the Mahalwari system resembled the Zamindari system in Oudh and C.P.,
while in Punjab it resembled the Ryotwari system.
However, the Mahalwari System also suffered from defects like the other two systems.
The position of the cultivators under this system was identical to the position of peasantproprietors, whether the Ryotwari system or tenants under the Zamindari system. It may be
observed that one of the outstanding features of all the three types of land tenure system was
that none of them arose out of the historical development of the Indian society. They were all in
the economic experiments by British rulers and completely wiped off all the remnants of the old

village communities. Summing up the position of the land tenures introduced by the English,
Marx observed: “In Bengal they (the British rulers in India) created a caricature of a large scale
English land estates: in South-eastern India a caricature of small allotment of property, in the
North-west they transformed the Indian communes, with common ownership of the soil into a
caricature of itself".
3.4.8 Disintegration of Village Economy
The overall impact of the East India Company’s revenue systems and excessive state
demand coupled with the new judicial and administrative set-up turned Indian rural economy
upside down with the village Panchayats deprived of their two main functions – land settlements,
judicial and executive functions – and the Patel merely acting as a Government official charged
with the duty of revenue collection, the old politico-economic-social framework of village

communities broke down. The introduction of the concept of private property in land turned
land into a market commodity. Changes came in social relationships. New social classes like

33
the landlord, the trader, the moneylender, and the landed gentry shot into importance. The
class of rural proletariat, the poor peasant proprietor, the sub-tenant, and the agricultural labour
multiplied in number. The climate of cooperation gradually gave place to the system of
competition and individualism. The prerequisites of the capitalist development of agriculture
were created. Further, new modes of production, introduction of money economy,
commercialization of agriculture, better means of transport and linkage with the world market
added a new dimension to Indian agriculture and rural economy.
These experiments in land settlements created a chaos in land relations and made the
peasants paupers. They also created social tension in the countryside and ruined the Indian
agriculture.

4.3 Commercialisation of Agriculture
A notable development during the British rule in India was the growth of commercial
agriculture. One of the consequences of the new land revenue systems and the demand of
land revenue in cash was that the old objective of village agriculture namely the production for
village use, was replaced by that of market. Also, there was a great demand for export crops.
Therefore the peasants tended to change over from the traditional subsistence crops to cash
crops such as opium, indigo, silk and sugar. The peasants began to produce for the requirements

37
of market. They did it with a view to realizing maximum cash which was needed to pay the land
revenue and to meet the claim of the money lender. This inevitably led to the emergence of the
phenomenon called commercialization of agriculture. Certain areas were solely used for the
cultivation of a single agricultural crop such as cotton, jute, wheat, sugarcane and oil seeds.
There had been a substantial increase in the acreage of indigo, mulberry, poppy and
sugarcane in course of seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. New crops like tobacco
and maize and a variety of edible fruits brought in by the Mughals and the Portuguese were by
now widely grown. Agriculture and horticulture in India were thus receptive to new items and
responsive to market demand. By the mid 18th century, development of market forces had

made deep inroads into the subsistence character of Indian agriculture. There was a substantial
growth of non-food crop production. Yet, farming technology was backward and stagnant which
was often the result of the poverty of the agricultural masses. But there was a very high yield
per acre in pre-colonial and early colonial days which cannot be simply explained.
With the rise of modern industries in England and growing demand for raw materials the
British government pursued economic policies which expanded the area of growth of such raw
materials as needed by the British industries. It was around 1833 that jute cultivation was
introduced in Bengal with a view to export it to foreign markets. A little later the export of cotton
was also started. Shifts in agriculture were most pronounced in river adjoining. The demand for

agricultural product, especially indigo, cotton, sugar and opium, caused shifts in cropping patterns
and expanded commercialisation.
The English East India Company and European enterprises played an important role in
the production of export commodities. They actually controlled the cultivation of cash crops like
indigo and opium. Sometimes they indulged in coercion. The exploitation of the indigo cultivators
by the European planters was a typical example for coercion. By the close of eighteenth century
when the export of indigo was steadily increasing, Europeans came to India and settled down
as indigo planters mostly in Bengal. They forced the ryots to cultivate indigo in certain portion
of their land and deliver plants to them at a fixed low price for processing. By receiving advance
from the indigo planters the cultivators became bonded. In the first half of the nineteenth

century indigo became a major Indian export and indigo planters flourished by exploiting the
ryots.
Besides indulging in coercion, the company also took steps to encourage the farmers to
shift to cash crops. The Company showed particular interest in the cultivation of cotton. Previously

38
cotton was cultivated mainly to meet the needs of the indigenous textiles industry. From the
last quarter of the eighteenth century, India came to be looked upon as a great potential exporter
of raw cotton to England. Therefore, the company took considerable interest to improve the
cultivation of cotton. Seeds of superior quality was imported and distributed to the farmers. In
the Madras presidency, Bourbon cotton was naturalized in the districts of Tirunelveli, Salam
and Coimbatore. Experimental cotton farms were set up to demonstrate better techniques of
cultivation. As a result of these efforts by 1857-58, Madras exported around 55 million pounds
of raw cotton. It should be noted that the increase in cotton cultivation often displaced the food
crops.
Normally, the growth of commercial agriculture would stimulate the peasant economy

because it provides the peasants with cash resources. But on the contrary the commercialization
of agriculture had adverse effects on the old peasant economy. This was due to the monopoly
of the Company and other European enterprises in the production and distribution of cash
crops. Sometimes the cultivation of cash crops had no connection with the traditional agriculture.
For example, the tea cultivation was largely isolated from normal agriculture. It was controlled
by the Europeans.
Further, the Company as well as merchants gave advances to cultivators to stimulate
production and control marketing of cash crops. These methods of advances and debt bondage
had taken away most of the profits leaving little to the cultivators. As a result, the Indian Agriculture
started suffering from stagnation and increasing rural indebtedness which had been more
explicit in the first half of the twentieth century.

4.3.1 Impact of the Commercialisation of Agriculture
Rural Indebtedness and Growth of Poverty – one of the most serious economic problems
in British India was the heavy rural indebtedness. The land revenue policies of the British and
the disastrous natural calamities like famines and epidemics brought economic miseries to the
agriculturists. A large proportion of Indian peasants got into debt due to their inability to pay
land revenue as a result of bad monsoons. In this situation the peasants depended on the local
money-lender. The village money-lender provided credit to the peasants. As he happened to
be the only supplier of capital to the peasants he pushed up the rate of interest to fantastic
levels. It was very unfortunate that there was no adequate substitute for the village moneylender.
The increasing burden of debt led to the growth of phenomenal poverty of the agricultural

population. The exorbitant rates of interest were not only unproductive but also a heavy burden
on the farmers. Unable to pay his debt and even interest on it, the agriculturist not only lost his
crops but also his land to the money-lender. The agrarian indebtedness had reached a high
level even in 1880 and went on increasing in the following decades. According to the Central
Banking Enquiry Committee report of 1931 the total agricultural indebtedness of the provinces
in British India was about 900 crores of rupees. The distribution of takkavi loans by the
government was too limited to deal with this vast and complex problem. The steady increase of
rural debt in India from Rs.3000 million in 1911 to 18000 million in 1938 was the clear evidence
of the worsening situation of the Indian villages. The consequent indebtedness ultimately resulted
in the transfer of land from agricultural class to the non-agricultural money-lender.

40
The increasing indebtedness of the agriculturists consequently led to alienation of their
lands. Under the pressure of debt they were obliged to mortgage and eventually to transfer a
portion of their land. It is to be noted that sale and purchase of land was rare in pre-British
times while it became common under the British rule. The Indigo disturbances in Bengal in
1860 and the “Neel Darpan” case had served to open the eyes of the educated Indians to the
degradation, oppression and poverty of the tiller of the soil. The Deccan riots in 1873 revealed
that the peasantry was living under a crushing burden of debt and required timely relief to
avoid an open revolt not only against the money lender but also against the government. The
Deccan Agriculturist Relief Act and the Punjab Land Alienation Act were passed not because of

government sympathy for the oppressed peasantry but due to political considerations.

5.5.1 Indigo Revolt (1859-60)
The indigo planters in Bengal exploited the local peasants by forcing them to grow indigo
on their lands instead of food crops like rice. The planters forced the peasants to take advance
sums and enter into fraudulent contracts which were then used against the peasants. The
anger of the peasants exploded in 1859 when, led by Digambar Biswas and Bishnu Biswas of
Nadia district, they decided not to grow indigo under duress and resisted the physical pressure
of the planters and their lathies (retainers) backed by police and the courts. The peasants
organised a counter force against the planters’ attacks. The ryots replied by going on a rent
strike by refusing to pay the enhanced rents and by physically resisting the attempts to evict

them. The Bengali intelligentsia played a significant role by supporting the peasants’ cause
through newspaper campaigns, organisation of mass meetings, preparing memoranda on
peasants’ grievances and supporting them in legal battles.
The Government appointed an indigo commission to inquire into the problem of indigo
cultivation. Based on its recommendations, the Government issued a notification in November
1860 that the ryots could not be compelled to grow indigo and that it would ensure that all
disputes were settled by legal means. But, the planters were already closing down factories
and indigo cultivation was virtually wiped out from Bengal by the end of 1860.
