14.3.2 Industrial Disputes in India during British rule
Before the First World War, industrial disputes were not very common in India although
strikes, rather loosely organised, did occur during the early phase of industrialisation. As early
as 1859-60, a notable scuffle took place between the European railway contractors and their
Indian workers. There is record of a strike over wages at Empress Mills, Nagpur in 1877,
between 1882-90; as many as 25 strikes took place in the Bombay and Madras mills. The
frequency of strikes, however, increased after 1905. The highest point was reached with the
six-day political mass strike in Bombay against the sentence of 6 years’ imprisonment on Tilak
in 1908. One of the most serious was in the cotton mill industry in Bombay city in 1924 on the
annual bonus; it involved over 1,60,000 workers and caused a loss of 7.75 million working

days. A further strike against the reduction of dearness allowance broke out in September,
1925. The mill owners restored the cut but not before the strike had caused a loss of about 12
million working days.
A strike broke out in Bombay in 1928 initially against measures of rationalisation and a 7
½ % wage cut but later extended to a wide series of demands. This strike, involving 1,50,000
workers, lasted for six months. In 1929, another general strike of Bombay textile workers broke
out under the leadership of the Girni Kamgar Union. This strike paved the way to the enactment
of the Trade Disputes Act, 1929. The strike lasted for 6-7 months and workers in all the cotton
mills of the city participated. A similar general strike, which occurred in 1929 in the Bengal jute
mills, was directed against the employer’s decision to increase the working hours from 55 to 60

175
per week. The strike lasted for 11 weeks, involved 2,72,000 workers and was withdrawn only
after most of the demands were accepted by the employers.

14.4.1 Legislations for the settlement of Industrial disputes
There was much legislation regarding the Industrial disputes. The earliest legislation
relating to the settlement of trade disputes was:
The Employers and workmen (Disputes) Act of 1860:- which was applicable to the
construction of railways, canals and other public works and provided for summary disposal of
disputes by Magistrates. Besides being limited in its application, the Act contained the undesirable
feature of regarding any breach of contract on the part of the workers as criminal offence.
The Trade Disputes Act, 1929:- was the result of the realisation of the increase in the

number of industrial disputes. The Act provided for the setting up of courts of Enquiry or Boards
of conciliation. The Court of Enquiry was to enquire into the specific matters referred to and
submit a report while the Board of conciliation was to endeavour to bring about a settlement
within a reasonable period of time. In case of failure, the board was to send a full report along
with findings and recommendations to the appointing authority. Sympathetic strikes were
declared illegal and provision was made for at least fourteen days notice for strike or lockout in
public utility services.
The Trade Disputes (Amendment) Acts, 1932, 1934 and 1938. The amendment
provided for the appointment of conciliation officers who were charged with the duly of mediating
in or promoting the settlement of disputes.
The Bombay Industrial Disputes Act of 1938:- was a pioneer legislation radically

different from the previous legislation on the subject. It marked the beginning of a labour judiciary
with its provisions for the creation of permanent machinery in the shape of an industrial court.
It was also passed which, apart from classifying the union into registered, qualified, and
representative, also provided for three distinct steps before a strike or lock-out could be declared.
First was the serving of a notice followed by negotiations. The agreement reached, the
contending party had to submit a full statement of its case. The dispute was recorded and the
chief conciliator submitted a report to the government. Finally, in case of failure, the government
could refer the dispute to a board of conciliation. During the period of conciliation, strikes and

178
lock-outs were declared illegal. So far, conciliation was not obligatory but now it was made
compulsory.
14.4.2 Legislations for the settlement of Plantation disputes
The Transport of Native Labourers Act of 1863 & the Transport of Native Labourers
(Amendment) Act of 1865,1870 and 1873:- The recruitment of labourers for tea gardens in
Assam was carried on for years mostly by contractors under the provisions of this act. Although
supposedly enacted for the protection of labourers under contract, the Act, in reality, benefitted
the planters. It made not only desertion but also indolence on the workers’ part a punishable
offence. Further, it empowered the planters to ‘arrest’ absconders within the limits of the district
in which they were employed.
The Emigration Act of 1882:- The existing laws having proved inadequate in meeting

the hunger of tea gardens for more and more men, the Government of India appointed a
commission of Enquiry in 1881 to deal with the problem on all India basis. The recommendations
of this commission led to the passing of the Act of 1882 which gave legal recognition to recruiting
agents and made the signing of a contract much easier.The Act is condemned as the ‘Slave
Law’, and was constantly assailed by the national press and the pitiful condition of gardenlabourers was lamented all over the country.
Labour and Emigration Act in 1901 & Labour and Emigration (Amendments) Act
in 1908, and 1915:- As a result of persistent agitation and constant efforts of Henry Cotton,
the liberal and courageous Chief Commissioner of Assam, the Government passed the Assam
Labour and Emigration Act in 1901 with the object of controlling and regulating the recruitment

of indentured labour for Assam plantations. Further amendments, passed in 1908, and 1915
abolished the system of indentured labour and withdrew the right of private arrest by employers
The Tea Districts Emigrant Labour Act of 1932:- It was the Royal Commission on
Labour which examined the question in considerable detail and its recommendations on the
subject formed the basis of the Act of 1932. The Act authorised the state government to declare
any area within a state to be a controlled emigration area and to grant license to any person to
act as a local forwarding agent on behalf of an employer/employers. The Act prohibited the
rendering of any assistance to children below 16 years to proceed to Assam unless they were
accompanied by their parents or other adult relatives. Likewise, no married woman could be
assisted to proceed to Assam without the consent of her husband. The Act further gave every

179
emigrant labourer and his family the right of repatriation at the cost of the employer after the
expiry of 3 years from the date of their entry into Assam.
14.4.3 Legislations for the settlement of Mining disputes
The mining industry employed a large number of workers many of whom were women
and children. Apart from the appalling living and working conditions, the industry was especially
prone to accidents in the absence of proper precautions. Till the beginning of the 20th Century,
there was no legislation to regulate the conditions of work in mines. The reason probably was
that the mining industry was largely foreign-owned and, unlike the cotton-textile industry, did
not compete with the British industry.
The Indian Mines Act of 1901:- was the first legislative attempt to regulate, though in a

half-hearted fashion, the inspection of mines and the employment of women and children. The
Act provided for the appointment of a Chief Inspector of Mines by the Government of India and
other inspectors by local governments.
The Indian Mines Act, 1923:- After a series of amendments, the Act was overhauled
and superseded by a more comprehensive Act in 1923. It fixed the daily hours of work of
persons, employed above ground, at 10 with a maximum spread over of 12 hours including a
rest interval of one hour after six hours work. The Act prohibited the employment of children
below 15 years while those below 17 were not permitted to work underground unless certified
medically fit.
The Indian Mines (Amendment) Act, in 1937& 1946:- gave powers to Inspectors to
issue orders to individual mines where danger was apprehended and to levy a duty on coal and

coke to defray the cost of rescue stations & provided for the maintenance of closed shower
baths, separately for men and women, at or near the pit-head.
14.4.4 Legislations for the settlement of Transport disputes
Indian Railways Act of 1890 & Indian Railways (Amendment) Act of 1930:- The
working conditions of railway workers were mainly regulated by this Act. Under the Act, the
hours of work of essentially intermittent workers were fixed at 84 per week and those of continues
workers at 60 per week. Provision was made for weekly holiday for all workers. Overtime was
to be paid at the rate of 1¼ times the ordinary rate of pay.

180
The Motor Vehicles Act, 1939:- As regards road transport workers, The Act, 1939,
regulated the minimum age of employment, hours of work and rest periods. The Act prohibited
the employment of any under 18 years as a driver of a motor vehicle and any under 20 years
as a driver in a transport vehicle and also limited the hours of work in the case of transport
workers to 9 per day and 54 per week and provided for a rest period of at-least half an hour for
every five hours continuous work. The Act did not cover such workers as attendants, conductors
and cleaners etc.
14.4.5 Legislations for the settlement of Dock Workers disputes
The Indian Ports Act, 1908 & The Indian Ports (Amendment) Act, in 1922 and 1931:prohibited the employment of children under 12 in handling goods in ports. Since 1937, the
minimum age for employment of children in docks was raised from 12 to 15 years.

14.4.6 Legislations for Social Welfare and Security
Workmen’s Compensation Act of 1923:- The question of workmen’s compensation
was raised as early as 1884 but it was in 1923 that the first Workmen’s Compensation Act was
passed. The Act, amended several times, applied to certain categories of railway servants,
workers earning Rs. 300/- (later raised to Rs. 500/-) per month and who were employed in any
capacity in factories, mines, plantations, construction activities, docks and certain other
hazardous occupations. The amount of compensation depended upon the nature of the injury
and the average monthly wages of the injured worker and ranged from Rs. 10-30 per month in
the case of temporary disablement, Rs. 500-4000 (now 4500) in case of death and from Rs.
700-5600 (now Rs. 6300/-) in case of permanent disability. The main drawback of the Act was

that it covered only permanent workers employed in specified occupations leaving out a large
number of workers exposed to risks. Besides, the compensation paid was too small.
The Payment of Wages Act in 1936:- As a result of the recommendations of the Royal
Commission on Labour, the Payment of Wages Act was passed in 1936 and it came into force
in 1937. The purpose of the Act was to ensure that wages were paid regularly and promptly
and that there were no arbitrary fines and deductions from wages. Under the Act, wages must
be paid on monthly basis. Establishments employing less than 1000 persons must pay wages
by 7th day of the month and, in other cases, by 10th of every month.
Provident Fund;- Schemes for old age pension or Provident Fund for workers in
government factories and railways were in force even before Independence. Many employers

181
like The Empress Mills, Nagpur. The D.C.M. Delhi and the Buckingham and Carnatic Mills,
Madras, Voluntarily provided this facility.
Maternity Benefits: The importance of granting rest and maternity benefits to expectant
mothers was brought home to the Indian public by the International Labour Conference which
adopted a child-birth convention in 1919. Efforts of N.M. Joshi to get a bill passed in 1924
proved a failure. However, on the recommendation of the Royal Commission on Labour, Maternity
Benefit Acts were later passed in almost all states. These Acts applied mostly to women employed
in regulated factories, mostly non-seasonal in nature, except in Bombay where it applied to
certain notified districts and towns. The qualifying period also differed from 150 days service in
Assam to 9 months in most other states. As regards the period of benefit, it varied from 7

weeks in Andhra, Madras and Orissa to 12 weeks in Assam Plantations, West Bengal and
Punjab.
Gratuity:- In the early decades of industrial development, many established industrial
enterprises followed the practice of paying cash gratuities to employees who retired after long
and meritorious service. However, it was voluntary in character and was treated as a payment
made by the employer at his pleasure. The position subsequently changed. Although no law
was passed but as result of a series of decisions of industrial tribunals, gratuity came to be
regarded as a legitimate claim which workmen could make and which could give rise to an
industrial dispute. In many cases, gratuity schemes formed part of contracts between employers
and labour unions or were prescribed in the standing orders and thus constituted a condition of

service. The practice of paying gratuity was widely prevalent in the railways, ports, docks, post,
telephones and telegraph departments, a few local bodies, insurance, banking, cement, sugar,
cotton and jute textile industries.

14.5 Growth of Trade Union Movements
A trade union is a voluntary organization of workers formed for the purpose of promoting
and protecting the interest of workers through collective action. Modern industrial sector in
India has a history of just 150 years. The foundations of modern industry in India were laid in
the middle of the 19th century. Plantation of tea, cotton and jute manufacturing, coal mining, all
started between 1850 and 1860. These newly-started mills enjoyed unrestricted freedom in
regard to the employment of labour and this understandably resulted in deplorable working
conditions as well as the association of women and children with factory work.
There were 25 important strikes recorded between 1882-90 in different factories of Bombay
and Madras. These strikes, which were more in the nature of protests generally ended in

defeat for the workers because employers were very powerful and workers were not yet united
and organized. For example, there was a ten days’ sweepers’ strike in Bombay in 1866; in
1867, the butchers of Bombay struck work. The plantation industry was the first to witness
“assaults and riots.” In the cotton textile industry, there was a ‘Protest’ strike in 1877 over
wages in the Empress Mills, Nagpur.
In September, 1884, two public meetings of textile workers were organised in Bombay
to protest against the wretched conditions of work in factories. A petition was adopted at the
meeting demanding a weekly holiday, half an hour’s mid-day rest, regular payment of monthly
wages and compensation in case of accidents. The petition signed by 5,500 workers was
presented to the president of the commission which was appointed to make recommendations

regarding the improvement of the Factories Act. This can legitimately be regarded as the
beginning of the labour movement in India.

183
The First Trade Union of Textile Works of Bombay came into existence in 1890. Since
then, several trade unions were formed. The Mohammedan Association set up in 1895. The
amalgamated Society of Railway Servants of India and Burma was formed in 1897. Soon
The Printers’ Union, Calcutta and the Bombay Postal Union were setup. The Kamgar
Hitvardhak Sabha, started in 1909. These early unions were of a sporadic or ad hoc nature.
Most of them had no regular constitution, no funds, no regular membership and no programme
of action.
The real beginning of the trade union movement in India was made towards the end of
First World War. The Russian revolution which took place in 1917 had its impact in India, there
were some other factors which especially favoured the growth of the movement. In the first
place, Mahatma Gandhi had come on the political horizon with his programme of achieving

independence for the country.The political movement, launched by him, not only brought political
awakening to the working class but also provided the services of educated intelligential to lead
it. Furthermore, the treatment meted out to Indian labour in South Africa created a stir in the
country and led to greater solidarity with the working class and the establishment of the
International Labour Office which lent a new dignity to the working class. It gave fillip to the
movement with the formation of Madras Trade Union set up by B.P. Wadia in 1918. The trade
union movement saw its real beginning by the country. All India Trade Union Congress
(AITUC) was formed in 1920. Again in 1922, All India Railway Men Federation & All India
Post & Telegraph Unions were formed.
The first trade union formed on modern lines was the Madras Labour Union in 1918. By

1920, there were 125 unions with a membership of 2.5 lakhs. The movement, however received
an unexpected blow when the Madras High Court, giving judgement in a suit field by Binny and
Company against the office-bearers of the Madras Labour Union, declared trade union activity
as an illegal conspiracy and restrained B.P. Wadia and his followers from further interference
in the working of the mill. The judgement came as a rude shock to the workers who realised for
the first time that they could be prosecuted also for genuine trade union activity. Thereafter, the
workers’ whole effort was directed towards securing legal recognition for the movement. N.M.
Joshi, the veteran trade union leader and a nominated M.L.A, brought the question before the
Assembly in March 1921. His persistent efforts in this connection finally bore fruit when the

Trade Union Act was passed in March 1926. Meanwhile, the year 1928 was one of great
industrial unrest and trouble. The government felt alarmed and took a series of measures such
as the appointment of the Royal Commission on Labour, The Trade Disputes Act of 1929, and
the appointment of the Bombay Riot Enquiry Committee. To cap it all, the government launched

184
the famous Meerut Conspiracy case in March in 1929 in which 31 trade Union leaders were
arrested in half a dozen cities on charges of conspiracy against the government.
The history of the movement from 1929-38 is the story of splits and unity. The All India
Trade Union Congress, witnessing dissension over basic policy matters, was split in 1929
when communists gained control of the organisation and the moderates left to form the Indian
Trade Union Federation. The movement was further split in 1931 when the extremists led by
Ranade and Despande left to form the All India Red Trade Union Congress. This was most
unfortunate and costly just at the time when the lengthening shadows of the Depression had
prompted wage-cuts and rationalisation. In 1933, more than 50,000 workers in Bombay city
were thrown out of employment and by 1934, almost every mill in Bombay had brought the

wages down. The workers’ strike in Calcutta, The Tata colliery worker’s strike and the Textile
workers’ strike in Bombay all ended in failure.
The communists launched the general strike in 1934 against rationalisation in Bombay,
Nagpur and Sholapur. The government came down with the Emergency powers Ordinance
under which the communist party was banned and more than a dozen registered trade unions
declared illegal. Some strike leaders were detained and others prosecuted under the Trade
Disputes Act. Thus, the labour movement was shattered in sprits, its leaders removed and its
ranks divided. This made the climate favourable for complete unity in its ranks. In 1935, the
Red Trade Union Congress merged with the All India Trade Union Congress; later Congress
Socialist Party merged and the National Trade Union Federation merged with the All India
Trade Union Congress in 1938.

The Government of India Act, 1935, allotted 10 seats in the Federal and 38 in the Provincial
Assemblies to labour representatives to be elected by registered unions. This encouraged the
unions to register themselves. The installation of popular Congress ministries in 1937 gave a
further boost to the movement. The greater freedom enjoyed by the workers and the sympathies

185
obtained by them from the Congress ministries in the assertion of their right to organise led to
a remarkable growth of the movement. By 1938-1939, the number of registered unions rose to
562 and their membership to 3,99,159. The number of registered unions which grew from 562
in 1939 to 865 in 1945 while the membership of unions submitting returns increased during the
period from 3,99,159 to 8,89,388. A notable development in the immediate post-war period
was the formation of Indian National Trade Union Congress on 4 May 1947. Soon afterwards,
in 1948, the Congress socialists also left the A.I.I.U.C. to merge with the National Federation of
Labour and formed the Hind Mazdoor Sabha. The establishment of these Unions led to the
final parting of ways between diverse political groups which had so far worked together.
14.5.1 Trade Union Act of 1926

Under the Act, any seven persons could form a union and have it registered with the
government. Registration, however, was not compulsory although certain privileges were
conferred on registered unions. The Act required a registered union to define its name and the
objects for which it was established. It was further required to keep a list of members and
provide for regular audit of its funds. The Act provided that not less than half the office bearers
must be employed in the factory/industry covered by the Union. Against these restrictions, the
Act granted protection to trade union workers against civil and criminal action for genuine trade
union activity. A registered trade union was permitted to create a fund, purely on voluntary
basis, for the promotion of civil and political interests of its members. The passing of the Act

was great landmark in the history of the trade union movement. The fear of prosecution being
over, unions began to be formed in large numbers.
